items.definition: Standard option pricing models assume that percentage returns, not raw price levels, are normally distributed. Mathematically, this implies that the logarithm of price levels is normally distributed, i.e., prices themselves follow a lognormal distribution.
items.core_idea: Modeling returns (rather than prices) as normally distributed keeps prices from ever going negative, since price moves shrink as price approaches zero, while leaving no ceiling on the upside — a better match for how many real asset prices behave than assuming prices are directly normal.
key_points: Normally distributed returns imply prices are lognormally distributed
Under this assumption, prices can approach zero but cannot go below it
There is no upper limit on price under this assumption
Using returns instead of price levels makes it easier to compare price behavior across different commodities, e.g., natural gas versus electricity
Returns become undefined if the starting price is ever zero or negative, which is a real risk in power markets since electricity prices can go negative
relationships: Underlies the binomial tree and Black-Scholes option pricing frameworks
trading_implications: In markets where prices can go negative (e.g., electricity), the standard lognormal-return assumption breaks down and must be treated as an approximation
common_misunderstandings: Assuming the lognormal model is a safe, unqualified fit for electricity prices despite the possibility of negative prices

items.definition: The tendency for real asset prices to experience large moves in either direction far more often than a lognormal-return model predicts.
items.core_idea: Real-world shocks such as bankruptcies, hurricanes, and infrastructure failures cause extreme price moves more frequently than statistical models expect, so the market compensates by pricing out-of-the-money options with higher implied volatility than at-the-money options.
key_points: Lognormal models systematically understate the probability of extreme events, such as a stock price hitting zero
Real triggers for such moves include company bankruptcy/takeover, hurricanes, and physical failures like downed power lines
Out-of-the-money options are most sensitive to these large moves and are typically priced with higher volatility than at-the-money options
Traders refer to this mismatch between actual and lognormal-predicted tail risk as the fat tail problem
relationships: Related to the lognormal distribution assumption it undermines
trading_implications: Volatility should not be treated as flat across strikes; OTM options trade at a volatility premium to compensate sellers for underestimated tail risk
common_misunderstandings: Assuming a single flat volatility input (as in a basic lognormal model) is adequate across all strikes

items.topic: Continuous trading assumption and jump diffusion
items.definition: Option pricing models assume the underlying can always be traded continuously. Jump diffusion is the industry term for periods when a price jumps from one level to another without being tradable at any intermediate point.
items.core_idea: Because trading requires both a willing buyer and seller, the assumption of continuous tradability can fail in energy markets — sometimes no counterparty exists at the location where a trade is wanted, so the price can jump across a gap with no intermediate trade occurring.
key_points: Continuous tradability of the underlying is a core assumption behind option pricing models, and it can be a risky one
Trades require both a willing buyer and a willing seller at the same time and place
In energy markets it can be impossible to find a counterparty willing to trade at the exact location desired
Jump diffusion describes the case where price moves without a trade occurring at any intermediate price
relationships: Compounds the fat tail problem in energy markets
trading_implications: Locational/nodal power markets can see prices jump without a matching trade, which complicates hedge replication in illiquid nodes

items.definition: The same binomial-tree framework used to model underlying asset prices can also be used to model the risk-free interest rate over time.
items.core_idea: A constant interest rate produces an unremarkable, flat binomial tree on its own, but it becomes essential later as the risk-free leg combined with the underlying's tree to compute a fair option premium.
key_points: Example given: at a 5% interest rate per period, a dollar held at Time t is worth $1.05 at Time t+1
With constant rates the interest rate tree is not interesting by itself, but is later used to derive the correct option premium
relationships: Feeds directly into arbitrage-free replication pricing

items.definition: An option-pricing approach in which fair value is derived not by forecasting the actual future price, but by finding a combination of the underlying asset and a risk-free investment that reproduces the option's payoff in every possible future state.
items.core_idea: Because predicting a specific probability-weighted future price does not compensate the option seller for the risk taken on, the fair premium is instead computed as the cost of building a replicating portfolio — a quantity of underlying plus a quantity of risk-free investment — whose payoff matches the option's payoff exactly in both the up and down states.
key_points: Simply multiplying a payoff by its probability (e.g., a 60% chance of a $10 payoff giving $6) undercompensates the option seller, who bears more risk than the buyer if the price prediction turns out wrong
There are two unknowns — the quantity of underlying (A) and the quantity of risk-free investment (B) — solved from two payoff equations, one for the up state and one for the down state
B is eliminated first because its payoff is identical in both ending scenarios; subtracting one payoff equation from the other isolates and solves for A
Once A is known, substituting it back into either original payoff equation solves for B
The option's fair value equals the cost of buying A units of underlying plus the cost/value of B units of risk-free investment at the starting period
This method only requires a plausible distribution of future outcomes (e.g., a binomial tree), not an accurate prediction of the actual future price
relationships: Builds on lognormal price distribution assumption and the interest rate binomial tree
trading_implications: Option market-makers price and hedge options through replication/hedging rather than by forecasting price direction
common_misunderstandings: Believing the expected-value price (probability × payoff) is the fair option price; it ignores the extra risk borne by the seller

items.definition: A numeric walk-through showing that solving the replication equations, rather than using a naive probability-weighted payoff, produces a higher and more risk-adjusted fair option value.
items.core_idea: For an underlying priced at $100/unit with a 5% risk-free rate and a scenario with a 60% chance of a $10 option payoff, the naive probability-weighted value is $6, but solving the replicating portfolio requires 0.4 units of underlying ($40) financed partly by a −$32.38 risk-free investment position, giving a fair option value of $7.62.
key_points: Naive expected-value pricing (60% chance of $10) gives $6, which the author states undercompensates the option seller
The replication solution requires holding 0.4 units of the underlying
Cost of the underlying leg: 0.4 unit × $100/unit = $40
The risk-free investment leg values at −$32.38
Combining the two legs ($40 − $32.38) gives a fair option value of $7.62, higher than the naive $6 estimate
trading_implications: Confirms that proper replication-based pricing compensates the option seller more than a naive expected-value calculation would

items.topic: Extending replication pricing over multiple periods
items.definition: Multi-period binomial option pricing extends the one-period replication method by building a full price tree for the underlying, computing option values at the nodes nearest expiration first, and then working backward node by node to derive today's option value.
items.core_idea: Multi-period binomial pricing uses backward induction: option values are first known at expiration, and each earlier period's value is found by replicating (duplicating) the already-computed values one step later, repeating until the current period's price is reached.
key_points: Step 1: build a multi-period price tree for the underlying
Step 2: calculate option values at the nodes closest to the option's expiration date
Step 3: walk backward through the tree, computing each earlier period's option value by duplicating the next period's already-known values
The time step between tree periods can be made arbitrarily small — day, hour, or even minute increments
In practice, daily or weekly steps are generally sufficient to build a robust binomial tree
relationships: Extension of the one-period arbitrage-free replication method; precursor to the Black-Scholes formula as time steps shrink toward continuous time

items.topic: Black-Scholes formula as the continuous-time limit of the binomial tree
items.definition: The Black-Scholes formula arises from taking the binomial tree's time steps to their logical extreme — infinitely small increments — at which point the pricing problem can no longer be solved algebraically and instead requires calculus, yielding a closed-form equation.
items.core_idea: Shrinking the binomial tree's time steps toward zero converts the discrete, iterative replication procedure into a continuous-time calculus problem, producing a formula that can be solved directly by plugging in inputs rather than stepping through every tree node.
key_points: Taking a binomial tree to infinitely small time periods requires calculus rather than algebra to solve
This produces a direct pricing equation, replacing the need to iterate through each node of a binary tree
relationships: Direct continuous-time extension of the multi-period binomial tree method
